title: Barns: The Unit Nuclear Physicists Named as a Joke
h1: Barns — the sub-atomic area unit with a WWII origin
description: 1 barn = 10⁻²⁸ m². Nuclear physicists named it because a uranium nucleus is 'as big as a barn' at that scale. Here is where the unit shows up and how to convert.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

hero: A barn is 10⁻²⁸ m² — the effective 'size' of a uranium nucleus from a neutron's point of view. The joke stuck; the unit outlived the classified project that coined it.
body: During the Manhattan Project, physicists needed an area unit for nuclear cross sections that would not accidentally reveal the size scale in classified telegrams. They chose 'barn' as a wry code — the nucleus was 'as big as a barn' compared to the tiny cross sections expected. The joke unit became standard and still appears in every reactor calculation today.

> 1 barn (b) = 10⁻²⁸ m² = 10⁻²⁴ cm² (exact)
> 1 millibarn (mb) = 10⁻³¹ m²
> 1 microbarn (µb) = 10⁻³⁴ m²
> 1 outhouse = 10⁻⁶ b (real joke unit, occasionally used)
> 1 shed = 10⁻²⁴ b (also real)
## What a cross section actually is

A cross section is not a geometric area. It is the effective target area a particle presents for a given interaction. A U-235 nucleus has a geometric radius of about 7.4 fm — a physical area of 172 fm² = 1.72 b. But its thermal neutron fission cross section is 585 b — 340× bigger, because the interaction probability is dominated by nuclear resonances, not by geometry.

A thermal neutron traversing 1 cm of U-235 metal (density 19.1 g/cm³, atomic mass 235) encounters 4.89 × 10²² atoms/cm² per cm path. With a fission cross section of 585 b = 5.85 × 10⁻²² cm², the mean interaction rate per neutron per cm is 4.89 × 10²² × 5.85 × 10⁻²² = 28.6. In other words, a thermal neutron in bulk U-235 fissions within a fraction of a millimetre — which is exactly why enriched uranium goes critical so quickly.
1 barn = 10⁻²⁴ cm². It is not a real area — it is a probability dressed up in units. And yes, 'outhouse' and 'shed' are real units, in one paper each.

faqs.a: Cross sections in m² are numbers like 10⁻²⁴, which are painful to compare. Barns produce nice single- and triple-digit values.

faqs.q: What is a millibarn used for?
faqs.a: Particle physics reaction rates. LHC cross sections are quoted in fb (femtobarn) or pb (picobarn) — the collider produces so many collisions that even 10⁻¹⁵ b interactions are visible.
No, but it is 'accepted for use with the SI' by the CIPM specifically because nuclear physics refused to abandon it.
